idiom_name: Array<T>.map with inferred result type (+ Promise.then for the async context)
implementation_notes: TypeScript keeps the runtime's map and adds the static layer: Array<T>.map and ReadonlyArray<T>.map infer the result element type from the callback's return type, so the mapped value's type follows the mapper without an annotation, and the same inference carries through the readonly tuple and generator types the handbook documents in its iterator chapter. There is no map on T | undefined - the closest thing to an optional context - so narrowing, optional chaining with a default, or a library Option type is the substitute, and the async context keeps Promise<T>.then. The built-in methods are the default realization because the compiler already types them; a container class is only worth its ceremony when the codebase needs the abstraction itself.
pitfalls: A mapper returning a union widens the result type, and filter(Boolean) does not narrow it - a type predicate or flatMap is needed, and an `as` cast silently removes the check the pipeline relied on.
Types are erased: lazy iterator helpers and the emitted helpers depend on the target and lib settings, so code typed against lib.esnext.iterator compiles even for runtimes that lack the methods.

Array.prototype.map's callback receives (value, index, array): passing a two-parameter function such as parseInt is a type error here (unlike plain JavaScript) but the temptation to cast it away hides a real bug.

variants.name: fp-ts Functor typeclass (HKT emulation)
variants.idiom_name: fp-ts Functor: Functor<F>.map(fa, f); Option.map / Either.map instances
variants.implementation_notes: The only named Functor in the TypeScript ecosystem is the typeclass encoding: fp-ts declares interface Functor<F> { URI: F; map: <A, B>(fa: HKT<F, A>, f: (a: A) => B) => HKT<F, B> } and documents the laws it must satisfy (identity and composition, restated over Kind<F, A>), with Option, Either, Task, Array and ReadonlyArray supplying instances so a function can be written once over F. HKT is emulation: a URI plus module augmentation makes F<A> type-check as Kind<F, A> because TypeScript has no higher-kinded types, which is why the encoding shows up in signatures and error messages. Use it when the codebase genuinely abstracts over several contexts; for one context the built-in methods are smaller and add no dependency.
pitfalls: HKT is emulation: a context must augment the Kind registry (URI mapped to Kind<URI, A>), and without that the typeclass cannot be used at all - it is not applicable to arbitrary existing types.
Instances are passed explicitly (fp-ts is not implicit like a Scala or Haskell typeclass), so every generic function takes Functor<F> as an argument and every call site names the instance.

Doing ordinary collection work through the typeclass pays the dependency, the erased-type overhead and the indirection without benefit - the built-in array/Promise methods stay the default for concrete contexts.
